title: How to build a low-risk portfolio for short-term financial goals
description: Structuring assets for capital preservation on a 1-3 year timeline.
content:
When saving for a goal 1 to 3 years away—like a wedding, house down payment, or dream vacation—the standard advice to 'buy and hold S&P 500' is dangerous. The stock market can drop 20% in a year. If your goal has a fixed deadline, you cannot afford market risk. However, leaving cash in a 0% checking account loses to inflation. The solution is a 'Liability-Driven' portfolio using Cash Equivalents and Fixed Income. This guide maps specific assets to your timeline to ensure the money is there when you need it.

Key Takeaways

  • Return OF Capital First: For short-term goals, prioritize getting your money back over getting a return on your money.
  • Match Duration: If you need money in 12 months, buy a 12-month asset (T-Bill/CD). Don't buy a 10-year bond fund (which drops if rates rise).
  • State Tax Arbitrage: In high-tax states (CA/NY), US Treasury Bills often beat High-Yield Savings Accounts (HYSAs) due to tax exemption.
  • Avoid 'Reach for Yield': Do not buy corporate bonds or dividend stocks for short-term goals. The extra 2% yield is not worth the 15% downside risk.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Current US rates (2025) allow for 'risk-free' returns of ~4-5% using government-backed securities. This is a historical anomaly that savers should exploit. You don't need to take stock market risk to get a decent return right now.

The Asset Menu by Timeline

Where to park cash based on when you spend it.

Timeline: 0-6 Months (Liquid)

Asset: High-Yield Savings Account (HYSA) or Money Market Fund (SPAXX/VMFXX).

Why: Instant liquidity. No penalties. Yield ~4.5%.

Timeline: 6-18 Months (Locked)

Asset: Treasury Bills or CDs.

Why: You lock in the rate. If the Fed cuts rates next month, your 1-Year CD keeps paying the high rate. T-Bills save you state taxes.

Timeline: 18-36 Months (Inflation Hedge)

Asset: Short-Term Bond ETFs (BSV) or I-Bonds.

Why: Short-term bond funds offer a diversified mix of high-grade debt. Price fluctuation is minimal (rarely drops >3%). I-Bonds protect purchasing power if inflation spikes.

Building the 'Goal Ladder'

  1. Define the Date: "I need $30,000 on June 1, 2027."
  2. Work Backward:
    - Put 50% in a 2-Year Treasury Note (Matures 2027).
    - Put 50% in a High-Yield Savings Account (Monthly contributions go here).
  3. The 'Glide' to Cash: As the date approaches (3 months out), sell any marketable securities (Bonds/T-Bills) and move everything to pure Cash. Eliminate all final volatility risk.
  4. Automate: Use a 'Sinking Fund' approach. Auto-transfer $1,000/mo into the HYSA. Every time the HYSA hits $5,000, buy a T-Bill to lock in the yield.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why not just use cash?

Inflation. On $50,000 saved for a house, earning 5% ($2,500) vs 0% matters. That $2,500 pays for your movers. Don't be lazy with large sums.

Are Bond Funds safe?

Safe-ish. If rates rise, bond funds drop in value. For a precise goal date, individual bonds/CDs are safer because they mature at Par ($100). Funds don't have a maturity date.

What about a CD Ladder?

Excellent strategy. Buy a 3-mo, 6-mo, 9-mo, and 12-mo CD. You have cash maturing quarterly, giving you options if your timeline changes.
